## Discrete-ordinate solution of a layered column (cdisort, always on in a DISORT band) {#sec-ch03-ordinates}

### Summary

cdisort solves the plane-parallel radiative-transfer equation in a stack of homogeneous layers. It replaces the
angular integral of the scattering source by a Gauss sum over $2N$ directions, the *streams*, which turns the
equation into $2N$ coupled linear ordinary differential equations in optical depth. In each layer these have an
exact solution: exponentials whose rates are the eigenvalues of an $N \times N$ matrix, plus particular
solutions for the beam and for a Planck source linear in optical depth. Matching the layers at their interfaces
and the boundaries gives one banded linear system for all layers at once. Nothing is iterated, and the solution
stays stable at any optical depth because every exponential is scaled to be at most 1. It is the method of
Stamnes et al. [@reading01], whose equation numbers cdisort's own comments quote.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Fluxes of a layered column from the $2N$-stream equations, @eq-ch03-ordinates-do.

**Data.** Per layer $\Delta\tau$, $\omega$, $\chi_l$; per level $T$; boundary values; out: level fluxes.

**Placement.** One `c_disort` call per spectral point and column, inside `disort_impl`.

**Activation.** Always, in a `solver: disort` band; `nstr` sets $2N$ (default 4).

**Guarantee / limits.** Exact for the discretised problem; error set by $N$ and the moment truncation.

**Evidence.** The Tests layer below.
:::

*Local symbols.* $I(\tau,\mu,\phi)$ is the intensity [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,sr^{-1}}$, per band] at optical depth
$\tau$ (counted down from the top) in the direction with cosine $\mu$ (positive upward) and azimuth $\phi$;
$I^0$ its azimuthal mean; $\mu_i, w_i$ ($i = \pm1, \dots, \pm N$) the quadrature nodes and weights;
$\mathbf{I}^{\pm}$ the vectors $I^0(\tau, \pm\mu_i)$, $i = 1..N$; $\mathbf{M}$, $\mathbf{W}$ the diagonal
matrices of $\mu_i$ and $w_i$; $D$ the azimuth-averaged scattering kernel; $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$,
$\boldsymbol{\beta}$ the coupling matrices; $k_j$, $\mathbf{G}_j$ the eigenvalues and eigenvectors and $C_j$ the
constants of integration; $\mathbf{Z}_0$, $\mathbf{Y}_0$, $\mathbf{Y}_1$ the particular-solution vectors;
$\bar B(T)$ the Planck intensity integrated over the band [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,sr^{-1}}$]; $b_0$, $b_1$ its
coefficients in a layer; $q$ the layer index, 1 at the top as in cdisort. Symbols of @sec-ch03-band keep their meaning.
<!-- local symbols for the editor's notation table: I, I^0, mu_i, w_i, I^pm, M, W, D, alpha, beta, k_j, G_j, C_j, Z_0, Y_0, Y_1, Bbar, b_0, b_1, q (layer index; Stamnes writes p, which NOTATION reserves for pressure) -->

DISORT has no switch of its own in pyharp: every DISORT band runs it, with $2N$ = `nstr` streams. With
`onlyfl` set (every shipped YAML) cdisort computes the azimuthal mean only, which is all the fluxes need.
Its accuracy is controlled by $N$ alone; @fig-ch03-ordinates-e3 shows the error falling with $N$ in a test with a
closed-form answer.

### Derivation

Start from the plane-parallel transfer equation for a medium that scatters, absorbs and emits, lit by a parallel
beam of intensity $F_0$ from the direction $(-\mu_0, \phi_0)$ [@reading01, p. 2502-2503, eqs. 1-4]:

$$
\mu \frac{\partial I}{\partial \tau} = I - \frac{\omega}{4\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_{-1}^{1}
P(\mu,\phi;\mu',\phi')\, I(\tau,\mu',\phi')\,\mathrm{d}\mu'\,\mathrm{d}\phi' - Q(\tau,\mu,\phi).
$$

The phase function $P$ is normalised to $\tfrac{1}{4\pi}\int P\,\mathrm{d}\Omega = 1$ and expanded in Legendre
polynomials of the scattering angle with moments $\chi_l$, $\chi_0 = 1$. The source $Q$ is the thermal emission
$(1-\omega)\bar B$ plus the singly scattered beam $\tfrac{\omega F_0}{4\pi} P(\mu,\phi;-\mu_0,\phi_0)
e^{-\tau/\mu_0}$. Expanding $I$ in a cosine series of $\phi_0 - \phi$ [@reading01, p. 2503, eq. 5] separates the
equation into one equation per azimuthal mode. Integrating over $\phi$ keeps only the mode $m = 0$, because
$\int_0^{2\pi}\cos m\phi\,\mathrm{d}\phi = 0$ for $m \ge 1$. The fluxes therefore need $I^0$ alone, and cdisort
computes only $m = 0$ when `onlyfl` is set (`c_disort`, {{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_disort repo=pydisort >}}).
The addition theorem of the Legendre polynomials turns the azimuthal mean of $P$ into the kernel
[@reading01, p. 2503, eq. 6b with $m = 0$]

$$
D(\mu,\mu') = \frac{\omega}{2}\sum_{l=0}^{2N-1}(2l+1)\,\chi_l\,P_l(\mu)\,P_l(\mu'),
$$ {#eq-ch03-ordinates-kernel}

truncated at $2N$ terms. Its beam source is $X_0(\mu)\,e^{-\tau/\mu_0}$ with
$X_0(\mu) = \tfrac{\omega F_0}{4\pi}\sum_{l}(2l+1)\chi_l P_l(\mu)P_l(-\mu_0)$ [@reading01, p. 2503, eqs. 6c-6d].
@eq-ch03-ordinates-kernel, multiplied by the weight $w_j$, is the matrix `CC` built in `c_solve_eigen`
({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_solve_eigen repo=pydisort >}}) from the factors `GL` of `c_disort_set`
({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_disort_set repo=pydisort >}}).

**Discrete ordinates.** Replace the integral over $\mu'$ by the double-Gauss rule: $N$ Gauss-Legendre nodes on
$(0, 1)$, mirrored to $(-1, 0)$ with $\mu_{-i} = -\mu_i$ and $w_{-i} = w_i$. The azimuthal-mean equation becomes,
for $i = \pm1, \dots, \pm N$ [@reading01, p. 2503, eq. 7a],

$$
\mu_i \frac{\mathrm{d}I^0(\tau,\mu_i)}{\mathrm{d}\tau} = I^0(\tau,\mu_i)
- \sum_{j=\pm1}^{\pm N} w_j\,D(\mu_i,\mu_j)\,I^0(\tau,\mu_j) - Q^0(\tau,\mu_i).
$$ {#eq-ch03-ordinates-do}

The nodes come from `c_gaussian_quadrature` ({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_gaussian_quadrature repo=pydisort >}}),
called and mirrored in `c_disort_set`. The rule integrates every polynomial of degree up to $2N-1$ exactly on each
half-range. The kernel is such a polynomial in $\mu'$, so $\sum_j w_j D(\mu_i,\mu_j) = \omega$ exactly: the
quadrature scatters no energy away [@reading01, p. 2504, eq. 7c].

**Matrix form.** Write @eq-ch03-ordinates-do separately for the upward directions $+\mu_i$ and the downward ones
$-\mu_i$, $i = 1..N$. Because $P_l(-x)P_l(-y) = P_l(x)P_l(y)$, the kernel has only two distinct blocks,
$\mathbf{D}^{+}_{ij} = D(\mu_i,\mu_j) = D(-\mu_i,-\mu_j)$ and
$\mathbf{D}^{-}_{ij} = D(\mu_i,-\mu_j) = D(-\mu_i,\mu_j)$. Dividing the upward rows by $\mu_i$ and the downward
rows by $-\mu_i$:

$$
\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{I}^{+}}{\mathrm{d}\tau} &= \mathbf{M}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{I}^{+} -
\mathbf{D}^{+}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{I}^{+}
- \mathbf{D}^{-}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{I}^{-} - \mathbf{Q}^{+}\right), \\ \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{I}^{-}}{\mathrm{d}\tau}
  &= -\mathbf{M}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{I}^{-} - \mathbf{D}^{-}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{I}^{+}
- \mathbf{D}^{+}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{I}^{-} - \mathbf{Q}^{-}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

With $\boldsymbol{\alpha} = \mathbf{M}^{-1}(\mathbf{D}^{+}\mathbf{W} - \mathbf{1})$ and
$\boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{D}^{-}\mathbf{W}$ [@reading01, p. 2503-2504, eq. 7b] the two lines
read

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\tau}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}^{+}\\ \mathbf{I}^{-}\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}-\boldsymbol{\alpha} & -\boldsymbol{\beta}\\ \boldsymbol{\beta} & \boldsymbol{\alpha}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{I}^{+}\\ \mathbf{I}^{-}\end{bmatrix}
- \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{Q}^{+}\\ -\mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{Q}^{-}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Homogeneous solution.** Try $\mathbf{I}^{\pm} = \mathbf{G}^{\pm}e^{-k\tau}$ with no source. The derivative is
$-k\,\mathbf{I}^{\pm}$, so

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\alpha} & \boldsymbol{\beta}\\ -\boldsymbol{\beta} & -\boldsymbol{\alpha}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{G}^{+}\\ \mathbf{G}^{-}\end{bmatrix} = k\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{G}^{+}\\
\mathbf{G}^{-}\end{bmatrix},
$$

a $2N \times 2N$ eigenproblem [@reading01, p. 2504, eq. 8b]. Its order halves. Adding the two block rows gives
the first line below, subtracting them the second, and multiplying the second by $(\boldsymbol{\alpha} -
\boldsymbol{\beta})$ and using the first gives the third [@reading01, p. 2504, eqs. 8c-8e]:

$$
\begin{aligned} (\boldsymbol{\alpha}-\boldsymbol{\beta})(\mathbf{G}^{+}-\mathbf{G}^{-}) &=
k\,(\mathbf{G}^{+}+\mathbf{G}^{-}), \\ (\boldsymbol{\alpha}+\boldsymbol{\beta})(\mathbf{G}^{+}+\mathbf{G}^{-}) &=
k\,(\mathbf{G}^{+}-\mathbf{G}^{-}), \\
(\boldsymbol{\alpha}-\boldsymbol{\beta})(\boldsymbol{\alpha}+\boldsymbol{\beta})(\mathbf{G}^{+}+\mathbf{G}^{-}) &=
k^2\,(\mathbf{G}^{+}+\mathbf{G}^{-}). \end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch03-ordinates-eigen}

The eigenvalues come in pairs $\pm k_j$, $j = 1..N$. @eq-ch03-ordinates-eigen is computed in `c_solve_eigen`
({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_solve_eigen repo=pydisort >}}), in the transposed order: it solves
$(\boldsymbol{\alpha}+\boldsymbol{\beta})(\boldsymbol{\alpha}-\boldsymbol{\beta})\mathbf{x} = k^2\mathbf{x}$ for
$\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{G}^{+}-\mathbf{G}^{-}$ with the real nonsymmetric eigen-solver `c_asymmetric_matrix`
({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_asymmetric_matrix repo=pydisort >}}), takes $k_j = \sqrt{k_j^2}$, recovers
$\mathbf{G}^{+}+\mathbf{G}^{-}$ from the first line and $\mathbf{G}^{\pm}$ as half the sum and difference. The two
orders give the same $k_j$ (check [C2]).

**Beam particular solution.** Try $I^0(\tau,\mu_i) = Z_0(\mu_i)\,e^{-\tau/\mu_0}$ in
@eq-ch03-ordinates-do with $Q^0 = X_0 e^{-\tau/\mu_0}$. The derivative is $-Z_0 e^{-\tau/\mu_0}/\mu_0$; dividing
by $e^{-\tau/\mu_0}$ and moving every $Z_0$ term to the left gives, for every $i$ [@reading01, p. 2504, eq. 9a],

$$
\sum_{j=\pm1}^{\pm N}\left[\left(1 + \frac{\mu_i}{\mu_0}\right)\delta_{ij} - w_j D(\mu_i,\mu_j)\right] Z_0(\mu_j) =
X_0(\mu_i).
$$ {#eq-ch03-ordinates-beam}

@eq-ch03-ordinates-beam is computed in `c_upbeam` ({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_upbeam repo=pydisort >}}),
which solves it by LU decomposition and warns if the matrix is near singular (when $\mu_0$ is close to some
$\mu_i$; `c_disort_set` moves $\mu_0$ by a relative $10^{-4}$ when it equals a node).

**Thermal particular solution.** Within a layer cdisort takes the Planck source linear in optical depth,
$\bar B(\tau) = b_0 + b_1\tau$ [@reading01, p. 2504, eq. 9b with $K = 1$], with
$b_1 = (\bar B_q - \bar B_{q-1})/\Delta\tau_q$ from the band Planck values at the layer's two levels. Try
$I^0(\tau,\mu_i) = Y_0(\mu_i) + Y_1(\mu_i)\tau$ in @eq-ch03-ordinates-do with $Q^0 = (1-\omega)(b_0 + b_1\tau)$.
The left side is $\mu_i Y_1(\mu_i)$. Equating the terms in $\tau$, and then the terms free of $\tau$
[@reading01, p. 2504, eq. 9c]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j}\left[\delta_{ij} - w_j D(\mu_i,\mu_j)\right] Y_1(\mu_j) &= (1-\omega)\,b_1, \\
\sum_{j}\left[\delta_{ij} - w_j D(\mu_i,\mu_j)\right] Y_0(\mu_j) &= (1-\omega)\,b_0 + \mu_i\,Y_1(\mu_i).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch03-ordinates-thermal}

@eq-ch03-ordinates-thermal is computed in `c_upisot` ({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_upisot repo=pydisort >}});
the level values $\bar B_q$ come from `c_planck_func2`
({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_planck_func2 repo=pydisort >}}), which pydisort passes to cdisort in
`disort_impl` ({{< code src/disort_impl.h disort_impl repo=pydisort >}}).

**General solution and boundary conditions.** In layer $q$, between $\tau_{q-1}$ and $\tau_q$, the solution is the
sum of the $2N$ homogeneous solutions and the two particular ones [@reading01, p. 2505, eqs. 18-19]:

$$
I^0_q(\tau,\mu_i) = \sum_{j=1}^{N}\left[C_{jq}\,G_{jq}(\mu_i)\,e^{-k_{jq}\tau} +
C_{-jq}\,G_{-jq}(\mu_i)\,e^{k_{jq}\tau}\right] + Z_{0q}(\mu_i)\,e^{-\tau/\mu_0} + Y_{0q}(\mu_i) +
Y_{1q}(\mu_i)\,\tau.
$$

The $2NL$ constants $C_{\pm jq}$ follow from $2NL$ conditions [@reading01, p. 2505, eqs. 17a-17d]: $N$ at the top,
where the downward intensity is the isotropic `fisot` plus the band Planck intensity at `ttemp` times `temis`;
$2N$ at each of the $L - 1$ interfaces, where all $2N$ intensities are continuous; and $N$ at the bottom. For the
Lambertian surface pyharp uses (`lamber`), the bottom condition is the $m = 0$ case of
[@reading01, p. 2505, eqs. 12 and 17d] with constant reflectivity $A_{\mathrm{s}}$ and emissivity
$1 - A_{\mathrm{s}}$ (Kirchhoff):

$$
I^0(\tau_L,\mu_i) = (1-A_{\mathrm{s}})\,\bar B(T_{\mathrm{s}}) + 2A_{\mathrm{s}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}
w_j\mu_j\,I^0(\tau_L,-\mu_j) + \frac{A_{\mathrm{s}}}{\pi}\,\mu_0F_0\,e^{-\tau_L/\mu_0}, \quad i = 1..N,
$$ {#eq-ch03-ordinates-surface}

where $T_{\mathrm{s}}$ is `btemp`. @eq-ch03-ordinates-surface enters the matrix in `c_set_matrix`
({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_set_matrix repo=pydisort >}}) and the right-hand side in `c_solve0`
({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_solve0 repo=pydisort >}}), with the reflectivity and emissivity set in
`c_surface_bidir` ({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_surface_bidir repo=pydisort >}}).

**Scaling.** The $e^{k_{jq}\tau}$ terms overflow in a thick layer. Substituting
$C_{jq} = \tilde C_{jq}\,e^{k_{jq}\tau_{q-1}}$ and $C_{-jq} = \tilde C_{-jq}\,e^{-k_{jq}\tau_q}$
[@reading01, p. 2506, eqs. 22a-22b] gives the homogeneous part

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{N}\left[\tilde C_{jq}\,G_{jq}(\mu_i)\,e^{-k_{jq}(\tau-\tau_{q-1})} + \tilde
C_{-jq}\,G_{-jq}(\mu_i)\,e^{-k_{jq}(\tau_q-\tau)}\right],
$$ {#eq-ch03-ordinates-scaled}

in which both exponents are $\le 0$ inside the layer [@reading01, p. 2506, eq. 23]. Every entry of the
matrix is then at most of size 1 times an eigenvector, and the system is stable for any optical depth.
@eq-ch03-ordinates-scaled is used in `c_set_matrix` and in `c_fluxes`
({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_fluxes repo=pydisort >}}).

**Fluxes.** With $I^0$ known at the nodes, the diffuse fluxes are quadrature sums and the direct flux is closed
form:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_{\mathrm{up}}(\tau) &= 2\pi\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i\,\mu_i\,I^0(\tau,\mu_i), \\
F_{\mathrm{dn}}(\tau) &= 2\pi\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i\,\mu_i\,I^0(\tau,-\mu_i), \\
F_{\mathrm{dir}}(\tau) &= \mu_0 F_0\,e^{-\tau/\mu_0}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch03-ordinates-fluxes}

@eq-ch03-ordinates-fluxes is computed in `c_fluxes` ({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_fluxes repo=pydisort >}}).

**What is exact and what is truncated.** For layers of constant $\omega$ and $\chi_l$ with $\bar B$ linear in
$\tau$, the solution of @eq-ch03-ordinates-do is exact up to round-off: no step after the quadrature
approximates. Three truncations remain. The scattering integral is a $2N$-point sum, exact only for a phase
function with no moments beyond $\chi_{2N-1}$. The moments from $\chi_{2N}$ up are dropped;
delta-M (@sec-ch03-deltam) moves the forward peak they describe into the direct beam. The Planck source is linear inside
each layer, so its curvature costs an error that falls with the layer thickness. There is no formal order in $N$;
@fig-ch03-ordinates-e3 shows the measured rate. Checks: `ch03_ordinates_algebra.py` for the steps above,
`ch03_e3_slab.py` and `ch03_disotest.py` for the code (the Tests layer below).

### Numerical method

The unknowns are the $2N$ scaled constants $\tilde C_{\pm jq}$ of every layer, $2NL$ in all, stored layer by
layer. The rows are the $N$ top conditions, $2N$ continuity conditions per interface and the $N$ bottom
conditions (@fig-ch03-ordinates-matrix). A row touches the constants of at most two adjacent layers, so every
nonzero lies within $3N - 1$ diagonals of the main one and the matrix has $6N - 1$ diagonals
[@reading01, p. 2506]. cdisort solves it with the LINPACK band routines `c_sgbco` and `c_sgbsl`
({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_sgbco repo=pydisort >}}, {{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_sgbsl repo=pydisort >}}),
called from `c_solve0` ({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_solve0 repo=pydisort >}}). The cost is
$O(N^3 L)$ for the eigenproblems and $O(N^3 L)$ for the band solve, per spectral point and column.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ch03-ordinates-matrix
#| fig-cap: "Block structure of the boundary-value system for three layers and four streams ($N = 2$). Columns are the constants of integration of each layer; hatched orange blocks are the top and bottom boundary conditions, sky-blue blocks the continuity conditions at each interface, which couple two adjacent layers. White is zero."
#| fig-alt: "A square matrix of 12 columns. The top two rows touch only layer 1, the bottom two rows only layer 3; each interface has four rows spanning two adjacent layers. The nonzero blocks form a band along the diagonal."
#| echo: false
from pyharp_report.ch03.figures.fig_ordinates_matrix import make_fig
make_fig()
```

The order of work in one `c_disort` call ({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_disort repo=pydisort >}}) is: check the
inputs; set the quadrature, the delta-M scaling and the absorption-depth cut (`c_disort_set`); compute the level
Planck values; for each layer solve the eigenproblem and the particular solutions; build and solve the band
system; evaluate the fluxes at the requested levels. With `onlyfl` there is one azimuthal mode and no user-angle
intensities. All quantities are point values at the levels or constants per layer; there are no ghost values and
no iteration.

When there is no thermal source, cdisort drops every layer below the level where the absorption optical depth,
$\sum (1-\omega)\Delta\tau$, first exceeds 10, and sets the radiation there to zero
[@reading01, p. 2508, Sec. III.D]. This is decided in `c_disort_set`; disotest case 12 checks it, and a pyharp
shortwave band is subject to it.

### Code

| what | code link | symbol | switch |
|---|---|---|---|
| driver | {{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_disort repo=pydisort >}} | `c_disort` | always |
| quadrature, scaling, cut | {{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_disort_set repo=pydisort >}} | `c_disort_set` | always |
| eigenproblem | {{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_solve_eigen repo=pydisort >}} | `c_solve_eigen` | always |
| beam solution | {{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_upbeam repo=pydisort >}} | `c_upbeam` | `fbeam` $> 0$ |
| thermal solution | {{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_upisot repo=pydisort >}} | `c_upisot` | `planck` |
| band Planck | {{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_planck_func2 repo=pydisort >}} | `c_planck_func2` | `planck` |
| band matrix | {{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_set_matrix repo=pydisort >}} | `c_set_matrix` | always |
| solve | {{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_solve0 repo=pydisort >}} | `c_solve0` | always |
| fluxes | {{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_fluxes repo=pydisort >}} | `c_fluxes` | always |

: Code map of the discrete-ordinate solution (cdisort at the pydisort pin). {#tbl-ch03-ordinates-code}

1. `c_disort` checks the inputs and prints, rather than returns, every error it finds; with `quiet` it prints no
   warnings. pydisort ignores its return code (the Limits layer of @sec-ch03-band).
2. `c_disort_set` computes the Gauss nodes, mirrors them, applies delta-M (@sec-ch03-deltam), sets the
   absorption-depth cut, and moves $\mu_0$ by a relative $10^{-4}$ if it coincides with a node.
3. For each layer, `c_solve_eigen` forms `CC`, $\boldsymbol{\alpha}\pm\boldsymbol{\beta}$ and solves
   @eq-ch03-ordinates-eigen; `c_upbeam` solves @eq-ch03-ordinates-beam and `c_upisot` solves
   the thermal system @eq-ch03-ordinates-thermal.
4. `c_set_matrix` and `c_solve0` build and solve the band system, using @eq-ch03-ordinates-scaled for the
   exponentials.
5. `c_fluxes` evaluates @eq-ch03-ordinates-fluxes at the output levels; pydisort returns `flup` and
   `rfldir + rfldn` (@eq-ch03-band-flux).

### Tests

No ctest exercises this solver (the Tests layer of @sec-ch03-band). Three derivation checks do:

| test (ctest name) | what it asserts | tolerance | where the tolerance comes from |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ch03_ordinates_algebra.py` [C1]-[C7] | the derivation steps hold in numpy and sympy | $10^{-10}$ to $10^{-15}$ | round-off, per line |
| `ch03_e3_slab.py` [C1] | grey slab, 32 streams | $2\times10^{-4}$ rel. | outline acceptance |
| `ch03_e3_slab.py` [C3] | opaque limit set by $\bar B$ | $5\times10^{-6}$ | see the footnote |
| `ch03_disotest.py` [C1], [C2] | cdisort test problems | ratio in $[0.99, 1.01]$ | disotest's own rule |
| `ch03_disotest.py` [C4] | pydisort equals C cdisort | 0 | same code, same inputs |
| `ch03_disotest.py` [C5] | `c_planck_func2` accuracy | $5\times10^{-6}$ | its stated 6 digits |

: Tests of the discrete-ordinate solution (derivation checks; no ctest exists). {#tbl-ch03-ordinates-tests}

**Grey isothermal slab.** A non-scattering slab at 300 K over a black surface at 250 K, band 500 to
$700\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, run through `RadiationBand` in weight mode, has the closed-form fluxes
$F^{\uparrow}(0) = \pi\bar B(T)(1 - 2E_3(\tau)) + 2E_3(\tau)\,\pi\bar B(T_{\mathrm{s}})$ and
$F^{\downarrow}(\tau) = \pi\bar B(T)(1 - 2E_3(\tau))$, with $E_3$ the exponential integral of order 3. Over
$\tau$ from 0.01 to 10 the largest relative deviation is $3.69\times10^{-2}$, $1.02\times10^{-2}$,
$2.70\times10^{-3}$ and $1.30\times10^{-4}$ at 4, 8, 16 and 32 streams, inside the $2\times10^{-4}$ acceptance
at 32 streams.[^ch03-ord-e3] Between successive doublings of the stream count the error falls by factors of 3.6,
3.8 and 21, so no single order fits. For $\tau \ge 3$ the deviation stops depending on $N$ and stays at
$4.5\times10^{-6}$ ([C3]): that is the error of `c_planck_func2`, which uses the constants
$\sigma = 5.67032\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-4}}$ and $c_2 = 1.438786\,\mathrm{cm\,K}$ and comes out
$4.52\times10^{-6}$ below the CODATA 2018 integral on this band, while it matches its own constants to
$1.2\times10^{-6}$ (disotest check [C5]; on 2000 to $2500\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ the deficit is
$5.0\times10^{-5}$).[^ch03-ord-disotest] Pydisort 1.8.13 gives identical fluxes.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ch03-ordinates-e3
#| fig-cap: "Relative deviation of the DISORT band fluxes from the exact grey-slab solution against slab optical depth, for 4, 8, 16 and 32 streams; each point is the larger of the top upward and bottom downward deviations. The dotted vermillion line is the acceptance at 32 streams. Above $\\tau \\approx 1$ all curves meet the floor set by the band Planck integral."
#| fig-alt: "Log-log plot. The 4-stream curve stays near 1e-2 to 4e-2 up to tau 0.3 then drops; 8 and 16 streams lie lower; 32 streams stays below 1.3e-4 everywhere, below the 2e-4 line, and flattens at about 5e-6 from tau 0.1 on."
#| echo: false

```

**cdisort test problems.** pydisort ships the cdisort 2.1.3 test driver (disotest). `ch03_disotest.py` compiles
it with every call recorded, replays each case through the pydisort Python API and applies disotest's own rule:
every ratio of computed to reference value in $[0.99, 1.01]$. All 30 runnable cases with published references
pass (cases 1-9; largest relative deviation $4.6\times10^{-6}$, at the print precision of the references), and
so do the self-consistency cases 10b and 11b. Case 12b fails in pydisort exactly as in C, by design: it compares
a run with the absorption-depth cut against one without, below the cut. pydisort reproduces the C solver bit for
bit on every runnable case ([C4]). Seven cases cannot be run from Python: the BRDF cases 6d-6h and 7e, and 14b,
which calls the two-stream routine pydisort does not bind.[^ch03-ord-disotest] On pydisort 1.7.1, `gather_flx`
returns fewer rows than there are output depths when they are fewer than the levels, so for cases 4, 5, 6, 7 and 9
the check compares the direct and diffuse downward fluxes at fewer depths there than with 1.8.13; the upward and
total downward fluxes are compared everywhere on both. All of it ran on CPU.

Output `derivation-checks/ch03_e3_slab.pydisort-1.7.1.out`; pydisort 1.8.13 (tag `v1.8.13`, torch 2.10.0+cu126) gives the same lines. The [C3] tolerances: $5\times10^{-6}$ bounds the Planck deficit of [C5] of the disotest check on this band, and the 16- and 32-stream values must agree to $10^{-7}$, 2 % of that floor.

[^ch03-ord-disotest]: [sha: f34506f9d14ee7b1f2e1222775baa5093ae6967f; deck: `derivation-checks/ch03_disotest.py` [C1]-[C6] with the pydisort source at 8af15242a265a60ea6fb51c29d48e6688a63ab67; run: `derivation-checks/ch03_run.sh <python> <pydisort source> <pyharp source>`, CPU, double, gcc 8.5.0 -O2 for the C driver; Python 3.11.13, torch 2.10.0+cu128, numpy 2.4.6, scipy 1.17.1, pydisort 1.7.1]. Outputs `derivation-checks/ch03_disotest.pydisort-1.7.1.out` and `.pydisort-1.8.13.out` (header-only C++ cdisort, g++ 8.5.0 -O2).

### Limits

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
- Plane-parallel only, with a Lambertian surface: a pyharp band has no input for the pseudo-spherical beam or a
  BRDF surface (the Limits layer of @sec-ch03-band).
- The band Planck integral is $4.5\times10^{-6}$ to $5.0\times10^{-5}$ below the CODATA 2018 value on the bands
  tested, which sets a floor on thermal fluxes (the Tests layer above).
- In a band with no `planck`, layers below an absorption optical depth of 10 get zero radiation.
- No order of convergence in $N$ is established; the stream count a problem needs is measured case by case.
:::

Two behaviours of the pinned cdisort and pydisort are not reachable from a pyharp band, which reads only level
fluxes, and are recorded here as CANDIDATE defects for users of pydisort itself. **CANDIDATE:** `gather_rad`
sizes the intensity array from the options, not from the depths and angles cdisort chose, so with `usrtau` or
`usrang` off it returns wrongly shaped intensities, for example (2, 3, 1) instead of (2, 3, 4) in disotest case
10b (disotest check [P1]). **CANDIDATE:** `c_albtrans` ({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_albtrans repo=pydisort >}})
overwrites the first returned albedo and transmissivity with the spherical ones after printing the beam values:
case 13a prints an albedo of 0.54526 and returns 0.158858 (disotest check [P2]); pydisort refuses the `ibcnd`
mode that reaches it.[^ch03-ord-disotest] Not tested: CUDA, single precision, user angles through pyharp.
